"Why can't I go into the kitchen, Mummy?" Ira, fourteen, stood in the doorway, cheeks hot. "Dadi just shooed me out like I'm dirty."
Sarika put down the ladle. "You're not dirty, beti. A period is your body working the way it should."
"Then why the rule?"
"It's how Dadi was raised, and it matters to her. In her kitchen we'll respect it for now. But it doesn't mean anything is wrong with you."
"I've got cramps. And I'm starving."
"Then you sit on the sofa with the hot water bottle, and I'll bring your food." Sarika lowered her voice. "Tonight I'll show you the book I bought, the one that explains everything properly. Ask me anything."
Ira sniffed. "Can I ask Dadi why, too?"
"Gently. She might tell you stories from when she was a girl."

qa.a: The book she bought, the one that explains everything properly.

qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt, as if she were dirty.

qa.a: It is how she was raised and it matters to her, which is not the same as wanting to shame Ira.

I thought I had turned into something shameful overnight. I stopped visiting friends and cried in the bathroom with cramps rather than "make a fuss". Then Uma Masi came to stay. She didn't argue with anyone about the customs. She just said, "Beti, in this house we follow Nani's ways. But your body isn't dirty, and you deserve comfort." She bought me proper supplies and a warm pack, drew diagrams on the back of an envelope and let me ask every embarrassing question. I still keep some of the customs, out of love for Nani. But I don't feel ashamed anymore.
Damini

Swati, our right half, showed me her phone today. She has been tracking her cycle alongside her training log for months and has noticed that a few days each month she feels heavier, teary and slower off the mark, while the following week she feels unstoppable. She was worried I would see it as weakness. I told her it is the opposite: it is information about her own body. We agreed that on her low-energy days she will do skills drills and lighter conditioning, and push hard on her strong days. She will tell me with one word, "green" or "amber", so she needn't explain in front of the team. I will check in next month on how it is working.
Suraj

Cried at a dog food advert today. Actually cried. Then snapped at Dilnaz for leaving her mug on my desk, and felt awful. A week later I'm the girl who volunteers for every presentation. Seeing the pattern on the screen made me feel less crazy. It isn't weakness; it's just my rhythm. So next month I'm not booking the debate trials on those days. Early nights, lighter reading, a long walk. I told Dilnaz and said sorry about the mug. She said she's noticed her own low days too, and we're going to compare notes. Weirdly comforting.
Mahima

I asked, "Is this a period thing?" She went completely quiet. Then she said, "No. It's a you-cancelled-on-my-parents thing." She was right. I had used her body as an excuse not to listen. Now I just ask, "How are you feeling? What's going on?" Sometimes it's cramps and she wants the hot water bottle. Sometimes it's something I did. Everyone's different. passage: In the antenatal clinic waiting room, Vidya squeezed Divyansh's hand so hard he winced. A few minutes earlier they had heard the heartbeat, and she had laughed and cried at once. That evening her brother Pradeep arrived on the bus with a tiffin of their mother's rajma and sat by her cot. "Didi, you've hardly slept. Anyone would cry." Kamal listened. From that night he took the baby between feeds, walking him up and down the courtyard so Geeta could sleep. Pradeep stayed two days, washing clothes and making her eat. "If it keeps going or worries you, we'll see the doctor at the health centre," Kamal told her. Slowly, as the nights got easier, so did the tears.

qa.q: What did Pradeep bring on the bus?
qa.a: A tiffin of their mother's rajma.

qa.q: How did Geeta feel when Kamal's mother asked why she was crying?
qa.a: She felt misunderstood and even more overwhelmed, so she cried harder.

qa.q: What helped Geeta, and why?
qa.a: Kamal walking the baby between feeds so she could sleep, and Pradeep bringing food and doing chores; rest, food and reassurance ease these early days.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see his sister's tears?
qa.a: He sees them as a natural result of exhaustion, not ingratitude, and says anyone would cry.

grounding: Illustrates a new mother crying easily and feeling overwhelmed after birth, and rest, food, reassurance and practical help from family easing it.
